Isaiah 1: Isaiah prophesies in Judah "in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah" (Isaiah 1:1), about 740–700 BC, as Assyria expands west. Judah is described as a land with burned cities (Isaiah 1:7).
Isaiah 2: The vision concerns "Judah and Jerusalem" (Isaiah 2:1) and the mountain of the LORD's house. Under Uzziah, Judah had grown wealthy and well-armed (2 Chronicles 26:6–15).
Isaiah 3: The oracle addresses Jerusalem's leaders and the wealthy "daughters of Zion" with their fine jewelry (Isaiah 3:16–23).
Isaiah 4: A short oracle follows the warning to Jerusalem, promising cleansing and a canopy over mount Zion.
Isaiah 5: The song of the vineyard is followed by woes on those who "join house to house" and "lay field to field" (Isaiah 5:8), during Judah's 8th-century prosperity.
Isaiah 6: Isaiah sees the LORD "in the year that king Uzziah died" (Isaiah 6:1), about 740 BC.
Isaiah 7: Rezin of Syria and Pekah of Israel attack Ahaz of Judah, about 735–732 BC (Isaiah 7:1; 2 Kings 16:5). Isaiah meets Ahaz at the upper pool by the fuller's field.
Isaiah 8: Isaiah's son is named Mahershalalhashbaz. Isaiah warns that Assyria will flood past Syria and Israel into Judah "even to the neck" (Isaiah 8:8).
Isaiah 9: The oracle names "Galilee of the nations" (Isaiah 9:1), the northern lands Tiglath-pileser III took from Israel about 733 BC (2 Kings 15:29).
Isaiah 10: Assyria is called "the rod of mine anger" (Isaiah 10:5). The chapter traces an army's march toward Jerusalem through towns of Benjamin (Isaiah 10:28–32).
Isaiah 11: The oracle speaks of a branch from "the stem of Jesse" (Isaiah 11:1), David's father, and a remnant gathered from Assyria, Egypt, and other lands.
Isaiah 12: A short song of praise closes the first part of the book (Isaiah 1–12).
Isaiah 13: "The burden of Babylon" (Isaiah 13:1) begins oracles against the nations (Isaiah 13–23). It names the Medes as Babylon's attackers (Isaiah 13:17); Babylon fell to Medo-Persian forces in 539 BC.
Isaiah 14: A taunt against the king of Babylon is followed by oracles against Assyria and Philistia, the last dated "in the year that king Ahaz died" (Isaiah 14:28), in the late 8th century BC.
Isaiah 15: The oracle against Moab names its towns east of the Dead Sea, including Ar, Kir, Dibon, and Heshbon.
Isaiah 16: The oracle against Moab continues, with Moabite refugees at the fords of Arnon.
Isaiah 17: The oracle against Damascus also speaks of Ephraim. Assyria captured Damascus in 732 BC.
Isaiah 18: The oracle addresses a land "beyond the rivers of Ethiopia" (Isaiah 18:1). A Cushite (Ethiopian) dynasty ruled Egypt from about 715 BC.
Isaiah 19: The oracle against Egypt mentions the Nile drying up and princes of Zoan and Noph (Memphis).
Isaiah 20: In the year Sargon of Assyria's commander took Ashdod (Isaiah 20:1), 711 BC, Isaiah walks barefoot for three years as a sign against Egypt and Ethiopia.
Isaiah 21: Oracles concern "the desert of the sea" with the cry "Babylon is fallen" (Isaiah 21:9), then Dumah (Edom) and Arabia.
Isaiah 22: "The valley of vision" is Jerusalem. The chapter describes breaking down houses to strengthen the wall and gathering water from the lower pool (Isaiah 22:9–11), and names Shebna, the treasurer.
Isaiah 23: The oracle against Tyre, the great Phoenician trading city, names ships of Tarshish and Chittim (Cyprus).
Isaiah 24: Chapters 24–27 widen from single nations to the whole earth.
Isaiah 25: A song of praise speaks of a feast for all peoples "in this mountain" (Isaiah 25:6), mount Zion.
Isaiah 26: "In that day shall this song be sung in the land of Judah" (Isaiah 26:1).
Isaiah 27: The section closes with Israel gathered from Assyria and Egypt to worship in Jerusalem (Isaiah 27:13).
Isaiah 28: A woe against "the drunkards of Ephraim" (Isaiah 28:1), whose capital Samaria fell to Assyria in 722 BC, turns to Jerusalem's rulers.
Isaiah 29: "Woe to Ariel, to Ariel, the city where David dwelt" (Isaiah 29:1): Ariel is a name for Jerusalem.
Isaiah 30: Judah's envoys go to Egypt to seek help against Assyria, to Zoan and Hanes (Isaiah 30:1–4), in Hezekiah's reign.
Isaiah 31: "Woe to them that go down to Egypt for help" (Isaiah 31:1), trusting in horses and chariots.
Isaiah 32: The oracle describes a righteous king and the careless women of Jerusalem.
Isaiah 33: A woe against a destroyer is followed by a picture of Jerusalem's walls and towers.
Isaiah 34: The oracle names Edom and its city Bozrah (Isaiah 34:6).
Isaiah 35: The poem describes a highway called "The way of holiness" (Isaiah 35:8) and the redeemed returning to Zion.
Isaiah 36: In Hezekiah's fourteenth year, 701 BC, Sennacherib takes Judah's walled cities. His officer, the Rabshakeh, speaks from the conduit of the upper pool (Isaiah 36:1–2). The same account is in 2 Kings 18.
Isaiah 37: Hezekiah prays in the temple, Assyria's army is struck down, and Sennacherib returns to Nineveh, where he was later killed by his sons in 681 BC (as in 2 Kings 19).
Isaiah 38: Hezekiah is healed and given fifteen more years (Isaiah 38:5). The sign is the shadow going back on the dial of Ahaz.
Isaiah 39: Merodachbaladan king of Babylon sends envoys, and Hezekiah shows them his treasures. This Chaldean leader fought Assyria twice for Babylon's throne.
Isaiah 40: The book now speaks to Jerusalem after her "warfare is accomplished" (Isaiah 40:2). Chapters 40–55 address exiles in Babylon and name Cyrus (Isaiah 44:28; 45:1). Many scholars date them to the exile; traditional readings hold that Isaiah foresaw it.
Isaiah 41: God speaks of one "raised up the righteous man from the east" (Isaiah 41:2) and of the coastlands trembling.
Isaiah 42: The first of the servant passages (Isaiah 42:1–4). Matthew 12:18–21 quotes it of Jesus.
Isaiah 43: God promises to bring Israel back "from the east" and "from the west" and names Babylon (Isaiah 43:5, 14).
Isaiah 44: The chapter mocks idol-making and ends by naming Cyrus, who will say of Jerusalem, "Thou shalt be built" (Isaiah 44:28).
Isaiah 45: God calls Cyrus "his anointed" (Isaiah 45:1). The Cyrus Cylinder records Cyrus returning displaced peoples and their gods after he took Babylon in 539 BC.
Isaiah 46: "Bel boweth down, Nebo stoopeth" (Isaiah 46:1). Bel (Marduk) and Nebo were Babylon's chief gods, carried in procession at the New Year festival.
Isaiah 47: "Sit thou silent… O daughter of the Chaldeans" (Isaiah 47:5): a taunt against Babylon, famous for its astrologers and stargazers (Isaiah 47:13).
Isaiah 48: "Go ye forth of Babylon, flee ye from the Chaldeans" (Isaiah 48:20).
Isaiah 49: The second servant passage (Isaiah 49:1–6), addressed to the coastlands. Zion says, "The LORD hath forsaken me" (Isaiah 49:14).
Isaiah 50: The third servant passage (Isaiah 50:4–9): "I gave my back to the smiters."
Isaiah 51: The chapter calls the exiles to look to Abraham and Sarah and to the exodus through the sea.
Isaiah 52: Jerusalem is told to wake and shake off the dust. The fourth servant passage begins at Isaiah 52:13.
Isaiah 53: The fourth servant passage continues (Isaiah 52:13–53:12). Acts 8:32–35 records Philip explaining it to an Ethiopian official.
Isaiah 54: Jerusalem is pictured as a barren, forsaken wife whose children will be many, recalling God's oath to Noah (Isaiah 54:9).
Isaiah 55: An invitation to "every one that thirsteth" (Isaiah 55:1) promises "the sure mercies of David" (Isaiah 55:3).
Isaiah 56: Chapters 56–66 speak of the temple, the sabbath, and Jerusalem's restoration. Foreigners and eunuchs who keep the sabbath are welcomed to God's house (Isaiah 56:3–7).
Isaiah 57: The chapter condemns idol worship "under every green tree" and child sacrifice in the valleys (Isaiah 57:5).
Isaiah 58: The people ask why God ignores their fasting; the answer concerns oppression of workers (Isaiah 58:3–7).
Isaiah 59: The chapter lists injustice in the courts and streets.
Isaiah 60: Nations bring wealth to Zion, including camels of Midian and Ephah, gold from Sheba, and flocks of Kedar (Isaiah 60:6–7).
Isaiah 61: "The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me" (Isaiah 61:1). Jesus reads this passage in the Nazareth synagogue (Luke 4:16–21).
Isaiah 62: Watchmen are set on Jerusalem's walls, and the city is given new names, Hephzibah and Beulah (Isaiah 62:4).
Isaiah 63: A warrior comes "from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah" (Isaiah 63:1). The chapter recalls Moses and the exodus.
Isaiah 64: The prayer laments that "our holy and our beautiful house" is burned with fire (Isaiah 64:11); Babylon burned the temple in 586 BC.
Isaiah 65: God promises "new heavens and a new earth" (Isaiah 65:17).
Isaiah 66: The book ends with nations coming to Jerusalem from Tarshish, Pul, Lud, Tubal, Javan, and the isles (Isaiah 66:19).
